question: How can a posterior over a price be used to choose the bid that maximises expected return in The Price is Right Showcase?

results.claim: The prior is a Gaussian KDE over 313 past prices of the first showcase (2011 and 2012 seasons).
results.setup: Steve Gee's records via Davidson-Pilon; KDE-smoothed
results.quote: we have 313 prices for the first show

results.claim: Contestants overbid 25% (first) and 29% (second) of the time; bids are biased low.
results.quote: the ﬁrst contestant overbids 25% of the time

results.claim: Error (price - guess) is modelled as Gaussian with mean 0 and the standard deviation of diff; strategic bidding may overstate it.
results.quote: the variance of diff to estimate the variance of error

results.claim: A probability density is a perfectly good likelihood because only proportionality matters.
results.quote: a probability density is a perfectly good likelihood

results.claim: With a best guess of $20,000 the posterior mean is $25,096.
Player 1's optimal bid is $21,000 with expected return of almost $16,700 (above the guess, unusual).
Player 2's optimal bid is $31,500 with expected return of almost $19,400 (below the guess, typical).
Summarising the posterior by mean or MLE is often unnecessary; Bayesian methods pay off when the posterior is carried into a decision or prediction.
results.quote: carry the posterior distribution into the next step

limits: Both showcases are assumed to have the same price when computing the double win; error variance is borrowed from bids rather than guesses.
practices: Treat the historical record as the prior and the contestant's own guess as data (p.56-64).
Choose the action by looping over bids and weighting the payoff by the posterior (p.65-67).
Model the opponent from historical diffs, not from your own guess (p.66-67).

terms.definition: the continuous version of a PMF; a density is not a probability and is unbounded
an algorithm that takes a sample and finds an appropriately smooth PDF that fits the data
